extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, students of 18th‑century fiction, and readers studying narrative technique (Tristram Shandy)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Laurence Sterne's Tristram Shandy (digressive, meta‑narrative fiction). Useful for extracting implicit principles about narration, dialogue, tone, and characterization in comic/ironic prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let people tell their stories their own way
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative order and chapter placement may be casual or non‑linear; the author defends writing chapters out of strict sequence and allowing digressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator explicitly resists critics for writing chapter 84 before 77 and argues that readers should 'let people tell their stories their own way.' Use non‑linear ordering and digression as a deliberate stylistic choice rather than a flaw; justify irregular structure via narratorial voice or as part of the work's temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of 'empty' or apparently 'nothing' chapters
rubrics_metrics.description: A chapter that 'has only nothing in it' can still be respectable and is 'no way a proper subject for satire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not automatically discard or satirize chapters that seem to contain little plot; such quiet or 'empty' episodes can serve pacing, tonal contrast, or rhetorical purpose. Treat intentional minimalism as a valid device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understatement and restraint to convey emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Short, simple declarations (e.g., Uncle Toby telling Mrs. Wadman 'he was in love' as he sits) can convey depth by restraint rather than amplification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray strong feeling through modest, understated statements and small gestures instead of bombastic speech. Let characters' restraint reveal sincerity or awkwardness; avoid unnecessary amplification if the scene benefits from modesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone, inflection, and delivery matter in dialogue ('fiddlestick')
rubrics_metrics.description: One word pronounced with different notes, accents, or tones conveys vastly different meanings — the text claims fourteen thousand variations in which one may do right or wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing dialogue, attend to rhythm, inflection, and implied delivery: the same line can imply tenderness, contempt, mockery, etc. Use stage directions, surrounding description, or sentence rhythm to encode intended inflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of an 'accent of humanity' to elicit trust
rubrics_metrics.description: An empathetic or humane tone in questions 'lulls suspicion to rest' and permits more intimate or invasive inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an apparently benign, humane voice for interlocutors who need to extract information or move a scene forward; contrast this with the interior reactions of the target character to show manipulation, curiosity, or sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization through small gestures and domestic details
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are revealed by simple actions (looking down at a darning slit, laying a Bible on a table, sliding fingers across a palm) rather than explicit exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brief, concrete gestures, props, and domestic details to reveal class, temperament, social codes, and emotional states. Small physical actions often carry social meaning in comic and realistic scenes; choose them to imply background and motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta‑narration and visible authorial process as a rhetorical device
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator interrupts to describe throwing a slipper, pulling off a shoe, or apologizing for chapter order — exposing the writing process and the author's persona within the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ self‑commentary, apologies, parenthetical asides, or visible composition as a stylistic choice to create intimacy, irony, or comic effect. Such meta‑narration can justify digressions and shape reader expectations about structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic juxtaposition of lofty and trivial registers
rubrics_metrics.description: High subjects (siege of Jericho, theology, glory of killing) are mixed with trivial domestic detail and low comedy to produce satire and humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix grandiose language or themes with mundane domesticity to create ironic contrast; the collision of registers is a source of comic effect and satirical commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground digressions with concrete spatial and technical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete measurements, maps, and precise spatial references (e.g., measuring thirty toises on a map, pointing to Maes and Sambre) anchor digressive narrative in material reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When indulging in digressions, include specific, sensory, or technical details to prevent the scene from floating free; concreteness lends credibility and humor to otherwise digressive material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of plausible ignorance or naiveté for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' misunderstanding or lack of definitional precision (e.g., Mrs. Wadman asking 'what do you mean by a recovery?') is used to comedic and expository effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let characters' partial knowledge, pedantry, or literalness generate comedy and reveal social attitudes; such naiveté can also serve to present exposition without breaking voice or resorting to authorial summarizing.
